en: The Patriarch Dadian commented that *pāra* means "reaching the other shore. As the Sutra says: "To cross a river one must use a raft; once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed.

If a single person gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, exhausting all principles and perfecting their nature, they will personally behold their original face and suddenly realize non-arising.
One immediately ascends to the other shore. Once attained, it is attained forever; once awakened, one awakens forever. One will never again be born;

the cycle of rebirth ceases forever, and birth-and-death are eternally severed. One becomes a leisurely person beyond the mundane world, roaming at ease according to one’s nature, tranquil and blissful.
The single word "Esoteric" (Mi) is a metaphor for the Great Void, which is able to encompass all phenomena.
Within the Great Void, the myriad phenomena of the universe—both sentient and insentient—are entirely contained within it. All phenomena are alternative names for the mind;

they are divided into eighty-four thousand categories, and when expanded, they are infinite and inexhaustible. When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
"Extinction. This single word everyone possesses, yet none can see it for themselves; even when explained, they do not believe it. It is called the "Dharma-gate of a Single Word.
Sentient beings do not believe that this very mind is Buddha. Therefore, the Buddha employs many skillful means to point out to sentient beings so they may perceive their own original nature.
The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness (*tathatā*); one must personally perceive this True Suchness. The dense...
The yellow flowers are nothing other than *prajñā*. One must personally encounter *prajñā*.
Jia Shan said, "The Way is nowhere not present," and he also said, "When you see form, you see the mind. Sentient beings see only form and do not see the mind.

If one can investigate thoroughly, walking step by step, keeping this in mind at every moment, pressing against it until it is fully realized, and suddenly encountering it directly, this is called "seeing one's nature. This...
The nature cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. One must look left and right, turn one's head and shift one's gaze;
meeting "Him" everywhere: "He is now truly I, but I am not now He. If you can understand in this way, [you have realized it].
Only then can one realize suchness (*tathatā*). This nature is formless and signless; it is directly seen within non-seeing, and non-seeing is realized within direct seeing.
Free from all manifold characteristics, one beholds one's own original nature; this is called the wondrous path.
This sutra is the path for sentient beings to practice. This sutra has been inherently present within every person from antiquity to the present.
It is only because sentient beings do not awaken to it that they fail to have faith in it.

If you can have faith in this, then know that whenever you stir the mind or give rise to a thought, there is a true person who is constantly in and out upon the mass of flesh; here, one personally beholds this Bodhisattva.
To practice with ease and spontaneity is the cultivation of the Way. If one wishes to travel a thousand li, the first step is the beginning. Look at this first step: from where does it transcend?
If you know the place of transcendence, you will know the root source of birth and death. "Deep" refers to the point that penetrates to the very bone.
When the five aggregates are suddenly and thoroughly penetrated, not even a hair’s breadth remains; it is as if before the parents were yet born. As the Prajñāpāramitā says: "Wisdom..."
A person of great wisdom and insight knows that because there is birth, there is death. They should sit in contemplation and observe from where birth comes and to where death goes.
If anyone gives rise to this single thought, they will be able to draw near to a spiritual friend and discern the dharma of birth and death.
The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Now, people rely upon these to practice, constantly reflecting inwardly to perceive them.
When the five aggregates are purified to the point of exhaustion—pure, stark, and vividly clear—one reaches this state where one naturally comes to rest.

If one does not attain the emptiness of the five aggregates, one will continue to fall back into the realm of birth and death. This body of the four elements and five aggregates is like an inn; it is merely the host for a guest.
A person dwells there for a time; once the owner has departed, the house eventually falls into ruin, yet the interest remains constant.
Form and emptiness are of one kind: from the Buddhas above down to the ants below, each and every thing is fundamentally and entirely empty.
The eye is form and cannot see; it is only true emptiness that can see. The ear is form and cannot hear; it is only true emptiness that can hear.
These are divided into forty-eight thousand modes of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, yet they all ultimately return to the six sense faculties. Form and emptiness are not different;
this is the wondrous principle of true emptiness.
Because there is the eye, one perceives forms; because there are forms, one perceives perceptions; because there are perceptions, one perceives mental formations;
because there are mental formations, one perceives consciousness. Because there is consciousness, the six sense bases arise as designations;
following sounds and pursuing forms, one wanders through birth and death without ever finding rest. If one wishes to sever birth and death, simply...

Illuminated by a single root, all is immediately empty and still. Directly taking up one's own self prior to the void kalpa, there is stillness while constantly illuminating, and illumination while constantly still.
In stillness, there is nothing to be stilled; one sees only emptiness. In emptiness, there is nothing to be emptied.
The eighty-four thousand defilements and delusive thoughts cease all at once. Both person and phenomena are empty; the path of words—
Sever it. Where the movements of the mind cease, the stirring of a thought is already a deviation; any contrived arrangement is an error.
If you can thoroughly reach the bottom and be without dependence, directly taking responsibility for it, then there is neither person nor Buddha.
The four great elements and the five aggregates arise from that void and vanish into that void; they have no connection whatsoever with one’s own Dharmakāya.

Blending with the light of the mundane dust yet unstained by it, one alone is the Honored One within the three realms. Do you understand this body that remains indestructible like the void throughout long kalpas?
The shadows of bamboo sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir; the lunar disc pierces the sea, yet no trace remains.
The *dharmakāya* of sentient beings is pure, without flaw, without defilement, and without pollution. It cannot be destroyed, nor can it be burned.

Like a lotus flower that is unsullied by water, the mind is the essence of purity and emptiness. It does not increase in sages, nor does it decrease in ordinary beings; it is suchness, immovable and without [end].
It lacks nothing and has no remainder. Striking empty space with a staff, space does not feel pain; shattering empty space with a sword, space is not severed;

binding empty space with a rope, space does not remain bound; burning empty space with fire, space is not scorched. The essence of empty space is such that it abides in form yet space does not receive form;
it abides in sound yet space does not receive sound. The six realms and four modes of birth are all mere provisional names; they have no point of reception whatsoever.

There are these six sense organs that accord with sentient beings. Sentient beings are fully endowed with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The Dharma-body has a name but no form; when it is in the eye, it is called seeing;
when in the ear, it is called hearing; when in the nose, it is called smelling; when in the tongue, it is called speaking; and when in the hand, it is called grasping.
When the feet move and run, the entire body gives rise to its function; this entire body is the Dharma-body. It is not through the six sense organs that one guides sentient beings;
rather, one must personally see the Dharma-body. If one attains this personal vision, one transforms from an ordinary being into a sage.
These six sense objects all arise from a single faculty. Simply remove one faculty and reflect back upon it: from where do they arise?
If you discover the place where consciousness arises, you will realize that the body is not "mine. Once the self-body is no more, the eighteen realms are suddenly purified.
These eighteen realms exist because of the grasping at the existence of the eye-realm, which drags along the other seventeen realms to give rise to various evil karmas. Simply remove the eye-realm.
Reflecting inwardly, one sees that the six sense-faculties are all false and illusory, ultimately returning to decay and ruin; they possess no reality whatsoever.

They take the substance of empty space as their essence—tranquil, eternally quiescent, and beyond cultivation or realization. The *nāga* is always in samādhi; there is never a time when it is not in samādhi.

Without distraction or confusion, its solitary luminosity shines alone, like the autumn moon. Its radiance pervades heaven and earth, penetrating and brilliant, utterly transcending the sense-faculties.
Dust reveals the body of true permanence; it is not bound by words and letters. The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally and spontaneously bright.
Simply by detaching from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness.

All sentient beings wander and drift from one state to another; this is entirely due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Through kalpas they have endured suffering, yet suddenly they may awaken of themselves and sweep clean the ground of their minds.

When they no longer perceive a self-body, the body is exhausted and ignorance is exhausted; the sins of ten thousand kalpas, as numerous as motes of dust in a sunbeam, are all at once and instantly stilled.
Where there is a body, there is ignorance; evil karma brings darkness, turning one’s back on awakening and uniting with the defilements. If one can, within this...
Through each of these successive transformations, the ordinary person is the sage, and the sage is the ordinary person. Dwelling in the dust, one is not defiled by the dust;
abiding amidst desire, one is free from desire. Neither form nor shadow remains; not even a single hair's breadth is established. As the ancients said:

"There is not even enough space to set a锥 (chui—a small awl) upon. Such a person is called a "mindless wayfarer" (*wuxin daoren*). Do not say that being mindless is itself the Buddha; even "mindlessness" still leaves a gap of one [thought].
A heavy barrier. Do you understand? A single sheet of white clouds spans the mouth of the valley; how many returning birds lose their nests!
Once ignorance is exhausted, there is no more old age or death. Sentient beings are inverted and wander along with the flow of phenomena because they cling to a self and others;
thus their deluded minds are not extinguished. Through vast kalpas of dust, failing to eliminate the notion of self and other, they cling to sounds and forms and fall back into birth.

Death. Even when objects are present before one’s eyes, there is still arising and ceasing. For one who has seen the nature, there is no phenomenon before the eyes, nor is there the mind of a sentient being.
The entire body is utterly forgotten, leaving no trace. The eyes and hands of the whole person do not establish even a speck of dust.
The twelve links of dependent origination and the myriad practices of the six perfections are all suddenly and completely cast off at once.

There is neither suffering nor pleasure; neither accumulation nor cessation; neither the path nor its fruition. Reaching this point, cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet defilement is no longer possible.
One transcends directly and enters the stage of the Tathāgata. Do you understand? Dense bamboo does not hinder the flow of water; high mountains do not obstruct the flight of white clouds.

Free from various views, liberated and fundamentally without reliance, its self-nature is pure. In reality, there is not a single dharma; having returned to the root, one attains the essential meaning.
Moment by moment, it is empty and still—the substance of the great void wherein sound and form do not exist. Like the world, like space: such is the person of the Way who has realized purity.
To realize the emptiness of persons is called *bodhi*; to realize the emptiness of dharmas is called *samyak-saṃbuddha*.
Both person and phenomena are empty; this is called Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*).
By explaining according to this, one attains great wisdom, benefits sentient beings according to their capacities, and guides the multitude of deluded ones to reach the other shore together.
The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Essence and function operate in tandem, merging and uniting into one.
Without is purity; within is purity. Without is emptiness; within is emptiness. They are empty in their very substance. Before heaven and earth existed, this emptiness already was.

"Nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; named, it is the mother of the myriad things. In the Great Beginning and the Great Primordial, it cannot be seen when looked at, nor heard when listened to.
It cannot be heard; one cannot see it when approaching, yet its head follows after one, nor can its rear be seen. It is like a thousand lamps illuminating a room, their light filling it everywhere;
all illusions and transformations are entirely without obstruction. Going eastward, there is no end; going westward, there is no limit.
Moving vertically and horizontally with sovereign ease, it cannot be bound or restrained; even a thousand sages are powerless against it. If you wish to distance yourself from it, first sever greed.
Desire. Sentient beings cycle through saṃsāra, their delusions never ceasing; like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, they wander through the world with no end in sight.

If there is one who can penetrate this thoroughly, they will forever escape these inverted dreams and illusions. "Jing" (竟) means exhaustion; it is the method of ultimate exhaustion, a vast and penetrating emptiness.
All conditions suddenly cease; one transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. In seeing and knowing, there is no seeing.
This is *nirvāṇa*. What is *nirvāṇa*? Within the space of a mere inch, the Master is not seen; yet the vast, empty kalpas are entirely present in this very moment.
Emitting light and shaking the earth—both person and phenomena are illusory. One does not perceive a past, future, or present; the three periods of time are themselves empty.
It is not that consciousness is extinguished to become empty; the nature of consciousness is itself empty.
Non-arising is called *nir* (cessation); non-dying is called *vāṇa* (wandering).
This is the *pāramitā*, the treasury of the true Dharma-eye. All Buddhas of the ten directions rely upon this to practice, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment and realizing their own self-nature;
it admits of no transmission or bestowal. Were there any such transmission, it would be entirely the heterodox views of external paths. [The Six Generations...]
The Patriarch cultivated and realized for himself; he did not bestow a single dharma upon others.
"A" means non-existence; "nuttara" means supreme; "samyak-saṃbodhi" means correct and true enlightenment.

By cultivating and realizing based on these four characters, one directly transcends to the stage of the perfect and sudden holy fruit, where no names or designations are established. If one relies on one's own learning and understanding...

People may run about in pursuit [of it], yet in the end they achieve nothing. This mantra is likewise the mind fully perfected by sentient beings. Having attained this Dharma-gate, one possesses great supernatural powers;
returning to the truth and reverting to the source, the palaces of Māra tremble, the light of the mind manifests, and it shines universally throughout the ten directions.
Of all phenomena, there is none that can transcend this Great Illumination, the Unsurpassed Mantra. *Gate* means the emptiness of persons; another *gate* means the emptiness of phenomena.
Reaching emptiness where there is nothing further to be emptied, birth and death are forever severed, and one reaches the other shore together, never again to undergo rebirth;
therefore it is called *Pāragate*. One cannot be defiled by the dust and toil of the five desires, and returns to the original source.
Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning; thus it is said: *pārasaṃgate*. *Bodhi* is the beginning, and *svāhā* is the end.

One gives rise to the bodhicitta and practices with courageous vigor, transcending the triple world. There is nothing to be realized, yet one realizes; there is nothing to be attained, yet one attains.
It is a vast, pure realm of ultimate bliss; hence it is called *svāhā*. Upon reading this, one attains sudden enlightenment:
the three realms, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Concluded)
